paragraphs: The following assessments concern on-site line work practices for electrical power-line installers and repairers; they do not predict hiring, qualifications, authorization, or contract outcomes.

Electrical power-line installers and repairers turn power and distribution system installation and maintenance requirements into safely completed work: operating switches according to drawings and work orders, testing for voltage and grounding for isolation, climbing poles or using aerial lifts to install and maintain conduits, cables, conductors, transformers, and switching equipment, using instruments to detect and locate faults, erecting or straightening poles, tensioning conductors, laying underground cables, and recording and handing over work before and after operations.

Wholly fictional line-work sample: given a fictional distribution single-line diagram and work order containing 1 overhead line section, 1 pole-mounted transformer, and 2 work points requiring grounding, plus two exceptions—a customer without power and abnormal conductor sag in a span—write a power shutdown, voltage-testing, and grounding sequence, personal protection points, work steps, and exception records within 60 minutes. Do not use real grid information or unauthorized materials.

Sample outputs and reflection: check whether outage boundaries and work permission are verified first, whether voltage testing precedes grounding, and whether grounding and work records are retained. Then consider whether you can stay focused outdoors, at height, and around energized hazards, strictly follow safety procedures, and accept responsibility for your own and others' health and safety.

Electrical power-line installers and repairers install or repair cables and wires used in electrical power and distribution systems and may erect utility poles and light or heavy transmission towers. This page covers O*NET 49-9051.00, excluding related roles such as electricians, telecommunications line installers and repairers, and pipelayers.

entries: Work inputs: overhead and underground lines, poles and towers, conduits and cables, conductors and fittings, transformers, circuit breakers and switches, electric meters and service drops, and worksite and safety conditions.

Verifiable outputs: installation or maintenance completed to work orders, compliant shutdown and voltage-testing and grounding records, installed or replaced equipment and conductors, traceable fault location and response records, and inventories and handovers before and after work.

Illustrative workflow for de-energized maintenance (editorial synthesis): check work orders and line diagrams → confirm shutdown, permission, and safety conditions under site procedures → trained and authorized personnel perform protection, installation, maintenance, and testing under applicable procedures → authorized parties confirm restoration conditions → record, count, and hand over. Energized and near-energized work requires separate specialized procedures; this page is not a universal operating procedure.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether outage boundaries and work permission cover all work points, when to test for voltage and ground, whether energized or near-energized work exceeds personal authorization, whether conductor sag and loads are safe, and which equipment or line changes require dispatch or supervisor confirmation.

Environment and pace: outdoor work in varied weather almost daily, widespread use of safety equipment, and daily exposure to hazardous conditions or work at height in most roles. Responsibility for others' health and safety is high, teamwork is frequent, and some roles exceed 40 hours per week and include emergency repair duty.

Research inputs: O*NET 49-9051.00 occupational identity and official scope, tasks and work activities, work context and styles, and tools and technology. Use findings within the exact U.S. occupational scope; do not infer mainland China licensing, wage, or employment definitions.

Check first: outage boundaries corresponding to the work order and line diagram, whether work permission has been obtained and confirmed, whether all work points have been tested for voltage and reliably grounded, whether personal protection and insulated tools are compliant, and whether safety barriers and warnings are in place.

Complete workflow: check work orders and outage conditions, test for voltage and ground, install and maintain, test and handle faults, inspect before restoring power, remove grounds, and complete records and handovers. Do not proceed before the preceding stage is confirmed.

Related responsibility boundaries: this page covers electrical power-line installers and repairers only. Electricians handle building and customer-side electrical installations, telecommunications line workers handle communications lines, and pipelayers handle trenches and piping. Qualifications and final responsibilities are not interchangeable with this page.

Construction equipment operators operate earthmoving, lifting, and construction machinery and bear machinery-operation risks, generally without responsibility for power-line shutdowns, voltage testing, grounding, or energized work. Electrical power-line installers and repairers focus on installing and maintaining distribution and transmission lines and equipment.

Electricians handle fixed electrical installation and maintenance in buildings and on customer premises, mostly involving indoor low-voltage equipment. Electrical power-line installers and repairers handle outdoor high-voltage lines, poles, and transmission towers, with different voltages, methods, and safety procedures.

Pipelayers handle trenches, pipes, and water supply and drainage systems. Electrical power-line installers and repairers handle cables, conductors, and distribution and transmission equipment, with different work objects, authorization, and insulation protection requirements.

Plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters install indoor piping and heating systems. Electrical power-line installers and repairers handle only power and distribution line equipment and do not take on work across equipment categories.

Personnel with applicable qualifications and authorization still verify outage permission, equipment status, and site safety under procedures. Tools do not automatically grant work authority. First use a wholly fictional single-line diagram and work order for an offline checking exercise. Record judgments and review results; do not let unverified automation prompts replace site inspections.

U.S. Electrical Power-Line Installer and Repairer Pay and Employment Scope

U.S. national 49-9051: 2025 median annual pay of 95,320 USD and official median hourly pay of 45.83 USD; the 10th and 90th percentiles are 51,470 and 128,690 USD. Employment was 131,900 in 2025, with projected growth of 10% for 2025—2035, reaching 145,500 in 2035, and 10,900 average annual openings. Openings include growth and replacement demand, not current recruitment counts.

Wage statistical position: 2025 U.S. national occupational wage percentiles, not individual starting pay or take-home income. Some line roles involve overtime and on-call duty, but this does not establish that the statistic includes an individual's overtime income.

The 10th and 90th percentiles are positions in the wage distribution, not newcomer, experienced-worker, or individual take-home pay. The percentile table cannot identify the separate effects of region, experience, on-call duty, or union arrangements.

The current O*NET major industry table is labeled 2025: utilities 50%, construction 36%, and government 12%. Employer industry distribution is not industry wages or demand projections; explain occupational wages by industry separately using the BLS OOH 2025 subtable.

Current U.S. national employment is 131,900 in 2025, with 10% projected growth for 2025—2035. Bright Outlook is an occupational outlook label, not an individual hiring guarantee, and cannot be spliced with Chinese wages or qualifications.
Fit Signals: Start with Observable Work Behaviors

To assess fit, first consider whether you can follow safety procedures outdoors, at height, and around energized hazards, strictly follow voltage-testing, grounding, and work-permission requirements, collaborate with dispatch and teams, and accept responsibility for your own and others' health and safety. RIASEC and similar tools can only suggest hypotheses; they cannot replace actual task experience.

Positive signals: strong practical skills, understanding of line diagrams and work orders, focus under weather and emergency repair pressure, and willingness to record work procedurally and accept supervision and review.

Conditions requiring caution: discomfort with heights, energized hazards, or prolonged outdoor work; difficulty with overtime and emergency repair duty; or a tendency to skip voltage testing and grounding under time pressure.

Trial action: use a wholly fictional single-line diagram and work order to write a shutdown, voltage-testing, and grounding sequence, personal protection points, and responses and records for two exceptions. Ask someone else to verify using the records.

The RIASEC interest code is RC (Realistic—Conventional), emphasizing hands-on and procedural work. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence, qualifications, or authorization.

Editorial suggestion: use measures such as the Big Five for self-reflection and observe collaboration and safety behavior in actual line tasks. This page has no research on their predictive or comparative validity for this occupation; do not determine competence from assessment scores.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or safety qualifications; use them for self-reflection only.

Entry Paths and Capability Stages

In the United States, workers typically enter through on-the-job training or registered apprenticeships, commonly starting with a high school diploma or equivalent and gradually gaining the experience and authorization needed for independent work. O*NET shows most respondents have a high school diploma or equivalent; verify education and training requirements by employer and region.

In the United States, verify apprenticeship, employer training, and specific state requirements; certification does not automatically grant work authority. In mainland China, check the actual work category and special operations catalog. Listed special operations require specialized training, successful assessment, and an operator certificate. The absence of a direct O*NET code mapping does not imply no entry requirements.

Training records, manufacturer or industry association certifications, and job work authorization are different statuses. Certification does not automatically authorize energized work, work at height, or independent work. Stop work beyond qualifications and authorization and transfer it to an authorized party.
Entry stage: under supervision, practice basic climbing and fall protection, conductor and fitting identification, safety procedures, and tool use, and record the work process.
Evidence to show: use a verifiable work plan, safety checklist, and exercise records to demonstrate procedural execution and collaboration.
Next step: check the target role's apprenticeship, training, and safety procedure requirements, then verify installation, maintenance, and fault-handling skills in supervised real work.
Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience, take on more complex line and equipment work, train newcomers, or move toward work supervision, energized-line work, or grid operations.
Market Signals and Transition Directions

Current U.S. national projections for 49-9051: 131,900 employed in 2025 and 145,500 in 2035, 10% growth for 2025—2035, and 10,900 average annual openings. These are overall employment projections, not AI attribution, current recruitment counts, or individual opportunities.
The current O*NET major industry table is labeled 2025: utilities 50%, construction 36%, and government 12%. This is the distribution of employer settings, not a demand projection.

Editorial hypothesis for transition to construction equipment operation: site collaboration, tool checks, and hazard-zone awareness may transfer. Power-line work experience does not directly establish the ability to operate excavating, loading, or grading equipment.

Construction equipment targets require additional evidence of equipment control, site and ground-condition judgment, work paths, and machinery inspections. Power-line outage or energized-work authorization does not authorize construction equipment operation.

description.text: Electrical power-line installers and repairers install or repair cables and wires in power and distribution systems and may erect poles and light or heavy transmission towers. Tasks include switching and grounding for isolation, climbing poles or using aerial lifts, installing and maintaining distribution and transmission equipment, locating faults with instruments, stringing and tensioning conductors, and laying underground cables. Work is outdoors, at height, and electrically hazardous, requiring safety procedures. When evaluating this career, examine the complete workflow, responsibility boundaries, evidence definitions, risk controls, and observable entry-level work samples together.

title.text: Evaluating a Career in Electrical Power-Line Installation and Repair: Work, Entry, and Risk Boundaries

subject.name: Electrical Power-Line Installers and Repairers
subject.summary: Electrical power-line installers and repairers install or repair cables and wires used in power and distribution systems and may erect utility poles and light or heavy transmission towers. Work is mainly outdoors, at height, and around energized equipment, requiring strict shutdown, voltage-testing, grounding, and personal protection procedures and responsibility for one's own and others' health and safety. This page covers O*NET 49-9051.00, excluding related roles such as electricians, telecommunications line workers, and pipelayers.
